newsitem.title: FRANCE: Renault staff council clears path for legal action.
newsitem.headline: Renault staff council clears path for legal action.

text.p: The European staff works committee of carmaker Renault voted on Tuesday to allow its secretary to take legal action against Renault's plan to close a plant in Belgium, the company said.

The committee did not decide to launch legal proceedings, "but if we asked for a mandate, it's because the probabilities are strong that we will," said Daniel Richter, a spokesman for the CFDT union. The committee secretary is a delegate from the CFDT.
Richter said Renault had not respected "the spirit of the law", which required consultations ahead of an announcement such as the decision to close the Vilvoorde plant in Belgium.
He said legal action would certainly press for a "clearer interpretation" of the French law on the subject, which is the same as the European directive.

Renault said in a statement that chairman Louis Schweitzer met with the European staff works committee for an hour and a half. "The European staff works committee voted to approve a motion to allow its secretary to take legal action against the procedure put in place by Renault," it said in a statement.
It said Schweitzer reiterated the reasons for the closure.

Renault has previously said the closure is part of a reorganisation of its European car operations to reduce the number of models assembled at different plants, resulting in savings conservatively estimated at 850 million francs ($150 million).

It said it decided to close the Vilvoorde plant, which employs 3,100 people, because its labour costs were 25-30 percent higher than those in France, because it was not the pilot for a new model, and because it required big investments in its paints operations to meet European environmental norms.
"Mr. Schweitzer stressed that Renault had fully complied with Belgian law, European directives and the accord with the European staff works council," the statement said.
Schweitzer told a French parliamentary committee earlier on Tuesday that the company had complied with Belgian law in announcing the plant closure.

In a statement issued after Schweitzer's appearance, the parliamentary committee said he pointed out distinctions in Belgian law, which requires negotiations for staff cuts but not for plant closures.

While sticking to his decision, Schweitzer told the European staff works committee that he was willing to meet the Vilvoorde staff council or a Belgian trade union delegation and would not set pre-conditions.
